chapter_theme: The middle of the Mokkala debate: Neelakesi argues against the Buddhist teacher Mokkalan that trees and the elements have souls; he turns to attack the Jain view that a thing both lasts and perishes, that substance stands with its qualities and that a thing can be called inexpressible; she answers each and turns his dilemma of identity and difference back on the Buddhist aggregates, and they dispute milk turning to curd and gram to mash as examples of transformation.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist teacher, named as the Buddha's chief disciple, whom Neelakesi debates

367.reading: Neelakesi holds that trees have life by the same mark as we do, since they change with the seasons, and answers that the heat and cold Mokkalan offered to show her reason faulty work on us in just the same way.
367.nuance: The verse picks up an exchange already under way: Mokkalan has called her reason (ஏது) fallacious by saying heat and cold, not life, make trees change; she turns the objection back on the human body.

claims.claim: trees are living beings, as their changes with the seasons show

368.reading: If Mokkalan rejects the analogy by pointing to knots and heat in trees as mere alterations, she says, he has thrown down the truth that the changes of an embodied body are felt.
368.nuance: கிரந்தி is taken as a knot or swelling in the wood; the sense of the second half turns on that and on reading பார்ப்படுத்தாய் as 'cast to the ground'.

claims.claim: swellings and heat in a tree are changes of a living body, as they are in ours

369.reading: She meets the objection that withering does not prove life: a tortoise whose skin is unlike ours also withers, and the taro of the garden comes to its natural end, so withering belongs to the living.
369.nuance: The tortoise clause (தோலொத்திராமையும்) is hard to divide; the reading that it is an animal unlike us which still withers is a guess.

claims.claim: withering and coming to an end are marks of life in plants as in animals

370.reading: Neelakesi says that when the Jains argue trees have life because cut trees heal as cut bodies do, Mokkalan calls this an error and lists it among faults, like men risen in madness.
370.nuance: She reports his charge of fault only to mock it; the comparison to the mad is aimed at him.

claims.claim: a tree that heals where it is cut shows life as a wounded body does

371.reading: She compares his refusal to accept the souls her scripture names, the beings that have earth and the rest for body, to calling a land's people by the land's name, a confusion of the thing with what it lives in.
371.nuance: The simile of the land and its dwellers is compressed and its direction is not certain; the claim follows the Jain doctrine that earth, water, fire, wind and plants are bodies of one-sensed souls, set out in the sermon (77).

claims.claim: earth and the other elements are the bodies of souls

372.reading: Everyone calls trees the fixed beings (தாவரம்), she says, and he does not know even that; why does he ask 'on whose word do you say it' as if tying his robe?
372.nuance: The last line's jibe about the Buddhist robe (சீவரம்) and its knot is obscure; it seems to mock his demand for an authority.

claims.claim: trees are among the fixed beings, as common usage itself says

373.reading: If a human-born being had no more than a tree-soul's knowledge of the body, she asks, why would those who revere the Bodhisattva of that nature refuse to make a distinction where he is greater?
373.nuance: The verse seems to turn the Buddhist's own Bodhisattva, who passed through many births, against his denial that trees have souls, but the syntax of lines 3 and 4 cannot be fixed.

374.reading: Trees and the rest, even the shy plant that shrinks, live by feeding and die when they are not fed, as plainly as stingy rich men live on gruel.
374.nuance: நாணமுடைய மரம் is read as the plant that shrinks at a touch; the comparison in line 4 with misers who live on gruel is uncertain.

claims.claim: plants take food and die without it, which only living things do

375.reading: Shaken in his hold on his view that trees and the deluded alike lack lasting souls, Mokkalan tells her to set out her scripture, and he will search out the faults in its nayas and its means of knowledge.
375.nuance: The first two lines are hard; whatever their exact sense, the verse marks the debate's turn from the souls of plants to the Jain theory of knowledge.
375.event: Mokkalan, unable to hold his ground on the souls of trees, challenges Neelakesi to lay out her scripture so that he can attack its nayas and pramanas.

376.reading: Mokkalan tells her to hear the faults that follow from holding a thing both to stand and to perish, to be and not to be, to be one and to be different, the narrator noting that he did not know her side fully.
376.nuance: The narrator's remark that he spoke without knowing all her position (முற்ற மவளது பக்க மறிதலில்) is the work's verdict in advance on the attack that follows.
376.event: Mokkalan announces the faults he will find in the Jain view of things as both lasting and perishing.

377.reading: Mokkalan argues that if a thing must stay the same it can do no work, and if it perishes then what appears is new each time, so her thing is faulty either way.
377.nuance: Neelakesi answers in 378 that these faults belong to one-sided views. Line 2 (காயத்தின் றன்மைய) is not clear in its detail.

claims.claim: a thing that lasts cannot act, and a thing that perishes is replaced by a new one, so a thing cannot be both

378.reading: Neelakesi answers that the faults he listed cannot be charged against those who hold that things both stand and do not stand, are one and then different, have gone and have not gone, each in its own respect.

claims.claim: a thing that both lasts and changes, and is one and different in different respects, escapes the faults of either one-sided view

379.reading: Mokkalan says that since she calls the lasting qualities eternal and the passing ones non-eternal, a thing standing apart from both kinds of quality cannot be accepted.
379.nuance: Neelakesi answers in 380 that no one held the substance to stand apart from its qualities.

claims.claim: there is no substance standing apart from its qualities

380.reading: Neelakesi asks why, having granted that the lasting qualities endure and the perishing ones pass, he will not grant the substance, and who ever said that the substance bearing them was something not joined to them.

claims.claim: the substance is the bearer of its lasting and passing qualities and is not apart from them

381.reading: Mokkalan presses a dilemma: if there is no thing besides the qualities the thing is only a label; if the qualities are distinct, they are distinct things; if they are one, they are one; she must say which.
381.nuance: Neelakesi turns the same dilemma back on him in 382 and 383.

claims.claim: substance and quality must be either the same or different, and either answer undoes the Jain account

382.reading: Neelakesi replies that his own school lays impermanence, no-soul, endless suffering and impurity on all five aggregates, so her position does not clash with his path.
382.nuance: தூய்தன்மை is read as தூய்து அன்மை, 'not pure', which makes the four the Buddhist marks the Manimekalai also lists (அநித்தம் துக்கம் அநான்மா அசுசி). Her point is that the Buddhist too ascribes qualities to a bearer.

claims.claim: the five aggregates are impermanent, without self, suffering and impure

383.reading: She turns his dilemma on him: if there is no aggregate besides the noble truth it is a mere name, if they are different they are two things, and if both are names of one they are one; let him say which.
383.nuance: ஆரிய சத்தை is read as the noble truth (ārya-satya); if it means 'noble existence' the retort is the same in form. The speaker is named by the verb கூறினளே.

claims.claim: the Buddhist relation of the truths to the aggregates meets the same dilemma of identity and difference

384.reading: Mokkalan argues that if she says she will not say, she contradicts herself in saying it, and if she says it one way the faults already named attach to her.
384.nuance: The target is the Jain mode of the inexpressible; Neelakesi answers in 385. The second line's turns on சொல்லலன் are hard to follow exactly.

claims.claim: to call a thing inexpressible is itself to express it, so the claim defeats itself

385.reading: Neelakesi answers that a thing is not in another's nature and is in its own, and that its many qualities cannot be stated at once; that is the only sense in which it cannot be spoken, which those who do not understand words miss.
385.nuance: Line 4's 'outsiders' speech' (புறத்தீர் உரை) is not clear; it seems to say the charge is the outsiders' misunderstanding.

claims.claim: a thing exists in its own nature and not in another's, and is inexpressible only in that all its aspects cannot be said at once

386.reading: Mokkalan objects that if her scripture means transformation, then when milk becomes curd and the milk has not perished, the curd ought still to be called milk, which is absurd.
386.nuance: He addresses her by her eyes streaked red like a fish (சேல்). Neelakesi answers in 387.

claims.claim: if milk persists in the curd, the curd should be called milk

387.reading: Neelakesi says the substance is the mass of form, while milk, curd and buttermilk are names of its stages; the milk perishes and curd arises, so the thing has a threefold nature.

claims.claim: a substance persists while its modes, like milk, curd and buttermilk, arise and perish, so it has the threefold nature of arising, perishing and lasting

388.reading: Mokkalan says she holds the change of gram into a cooked mash as her doctrine, and demands that she show plainly some one thing apart in both states, or he will call it a turtle's hair.
388.nuance: 'Turtle's hair' (ஆமை மயிர்) is the stock example of the non-existent. Line 1's பயற்றியல்டே is corrupt. Neelakesi answers in 389.

claims.claim: no thing persisting through the change of gram into mash can be shown, so it does not exist

389.reading: Neelakesi says the lump that perished and the paste that arose are both the thing in its modes, which differ from each other, and she too affirms loss and arising for the form.
389.nuance: பையைகளேஎன்னும் in line 2 looks corrupt; it is read as naming the modes.

claims.claim: loss and arising belong to the modes of a substance, which differ while the substance remains

390.reading: Mokkalan retorts that if she wants changing things to become gram and mash by change, then gram poured with charcoal and water should also burn, and asks whether that is the same.
390.nuance: The verse is obscure and the answer falls in the next chapter, so the claim is marked reported here; the reading of கரியும் as charcoal is a guess.

claims.claim: if the persisting material makes things the same, mixtures with other matter would share each other's nature

links.note: The sermon told Neelakesi the fixed beings are of five kinds; here she defends that teaching against a Buddhist by calling trees fixed beings (தாவரம்) that everyone knows to be such.
links.teaches: The doctrine she received as a convert's lesson becomes the first ground she must hold in open debate, and she defends it by appeal to common usage rather than to the sage's authority.

links.note: In the Arkkachandra debate she named the felling of living trees among sins that bring hell; here she argues against Mokkalan that trees really are alive.
links.teaches: The earlier charge that felling a tree is a sin rests on a premise the Buddhists deny, and this passage supplies the argument for it: healing, feeding and withering show the tree to be a soul one can wrong.

links.note: Both use gram cooked into a mash (கும்மாயம்) as the Jain example of a kind that persists while its form passes; the Manimekalai lets the Jain state it unanswered, the Neelakesi puts it under a Buddhist's attack.
links.teaches: The same stock example served the two traditions differently: the Buddhist epic records it as the Jain's own illustration and moves on, while the Jain epic has a Buddhist demand to be shown the persisting thing, so the example's weak point is named by the side that wrote it down.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists impermanence, suffering, no-self and impurity as marks to contemplate in order to cut attachment; Neelakesi names the same four as qualities the Buddhists lay on the aggregates.
links.teaches: The four marks the Buddhist teacher gives as a meditation for release are read by the Jain debater as predicates of a bearer, so the Buddhist list is turned into evidence for the substance-and-quality relation Mokkalan denies.

links.note: Mokkalan says that to declare a thing inexpressible is self-contradiction; the Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher counts keeping silent before an ill-formed question as a proper kind of answer.
links.teaches: The Buddhist in the Jain epic attacks the Jain mode of the inexpressible with an argument his own school, as the Manimekalai presents it, would have to face, since it too treats not saying as an answer.

links.note: Mokkalan demands that substance and quality be declared either one or different; the Manimekalai's teacher gives a naya of oneness and a naya of difference as two valid ways of seeing cause and effect.
links.teaches: Mokkalan's either-or is stricter than the Buddhist doctrine the Manimekalai sets out, which itself allows a thing to be viewed as one with its cause under one naya and as different under another, close to the Jain answer he rejects.

links.note: The Kural likens men without kindly regard to trees fixed in the soil; Neelakesi argues that trees feel heat and cold and change as living bodies do.
links.teaches: Read with the Jain argument, the couplet's tree is not a dead thing but a living being that feels by touch yet has no eye to look with, which makes the comparison exact for a man who has eyes and does not use them kindly.

gains.a: the Jain claim that trees feel is seen against a Tamil commonplace that used the tree as the very type of the unfeeling
gains.b: the couplet's simile gains a precise sense under the Jain scale of senses: the tree lacks sight, not life

links.note: The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for what lasts; Mokkalan and Neelakesi dispute whether a thing can both last and not last.
links.teaches: The couplet assumes things fall cleanly into the lasting and the passing, and the debate shows that division itself was contested, the Jain holding one thing lasting in substance and passing in its modes.

gains.a: the debate's technical question is tied to a Tamil moral warning about mistaking the passing for the lasting
gains.b: the couplet's simple contrast is shown to stand on a metaphysical choice the schools did not share

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id differs from vaadham, which the list already uses for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: கந்தங்களைந்திற்கும் (382), கந்தம் (383)

new_concepts.gloss: a quality of a thing, lasting or passing, and its relation to the substance (பொருள், குணி) that bears it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: குணங்கள் (379, 381), குணம் (380)

new_concepts.gloss: transformation: a substance passing into new modes, as milk into curd, while something of it persists

source_issues: 372 line 2: the edition's '•' is the old encoding of ஃ (repaired in the core).
383 line 3: a TSCII leftover was repaired in the core (ேரி); the reading பேரிவை is kept.
389 line 2: பையைகளேஎன்னும் looks corrupt; the line's sense is doubtful.
390: obscure throughout; the reply falls in the next chapter.
367-374: no speech verb names the speaker; Neelakesi is taken as speaker from the story and the Jain 'we' (யாம், 367).
